data.title: US court blocks Trump administration bid to keep Michigan coal plant open
data.description:
By Nichola Groom

A federal appeals court on Friday threw out an order from President Donald Trump's administration that had forced a Michigan coal plant to remain open beyond its planned retirement.

The unanimous ruling by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found the Department of Energy exceeded its authority under a rarely used emergency provision of federal law, according to court papers.

Michigan challenged the order after DOE instructed the 1960s-era J.H. Campbell plant in 2025 to remain online shortly before its planned closure.

The ruling is a setback for the administration's efforts to preserve coal-fired generation at a time when U.S. demand for electricity has soared due largely to the expansion of data centers. Coal-fired power is among the largest sources of carbon dioxide emissions that contribute to climate change.

"By forcing its continued operation, DOE tried a never-before-used tactic to illegally prop up the aging J.H. Campbell coal plant that nobody asked to keep, sticking ratepayers with a bill for a facility that should have been retired more than a year ago," Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a statement. "I am relieved that the Court saw through this facade and threw out DOE’s order that had zero basis in reality."

Since 2025, the Trump administration has used emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep operating several aging power plants slated for retirement, including coal plants in Michigan, Indiana, Washington state and Colorado.

DOE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The decision comes a month after DOE extended the emergency order to keep the aging J.H. Campbell Generating Plant open through November 14.

The Consumers Energy plant had been slated to close in 2025 because it was no longer economic. Its continued operation under the order cost the utility $295 million from May 2025 through June 2026, according to the Michigan attorney general's office.

Consumers Energy is reviewing the ruling, spokesperson Brian Wheeler said.

"While that happens, we are continuing to comply with the current 90-day Department of Energy order that keeps the Campbell plant operating," he said.

Environmental groups welcomed the ruling.

“The DOE needs to stay in its lane and use its emergency powers only in actual emergencies," Michael Lenoff, an attorney with environmental group Earthjustice, said in a statement. "Preventing the market-driven retirements of coal plants to advance a coal-friendly agenda is not a proper use of emergency powers."

data.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy to shut Cove Point LNG export plant in Maryland for annual maintenance
data.description:
By Scott DiSavino and Curtis Williams

U.S. firm Berkshire Hathaway Energy plans to shut its Cove Point LNG export plant in Maryland around September 19 for about two-weeks to conduct annual maintenance, according to a company notice.

  • For the first eight months of 2026 it exported 3.58 million metric tons, according to data from financial firm LSEG. The plant can turn around 0.8 bcfd of gas into LNG.

  • The amount of natural gas flowing to the plant has averaged around 0.9 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) so far in September, according to data from financial firm LSEG. Plants often pull in more gas than they can turn into LNG since they use some of the fuel to run equipment.

  • U.S. LNG export plants typically shut for planned maintenance in the spring or autumn when global demand for gas for heating or cooling is lower than during the peak winter and summer months.

  • Berkshire Hathaway Energy is a unit of U.S. multinational conglomerate Berkshire Hathaway . It operates Cove Point and owns 75% of the facility. The other 25% is owned by units of Brookfield Asset Management (BAMa.TO).

  • Cove Point's LNG is sold under 20-year agreements to a subsidiary of GAIL (India) and to ST Cove Point, which is a joint venture between units of Japanese trading company Sumitomo and Tokyo Gas .

What Happened?

Shares of visual content marketplace Getty Images fell 2.3% in the afternoon session after JPMorgan initiated coverage on the company with an Underweight rating, according to Streetinsider. An Underweight rating indicates that the investment firm expects the stock to underperform relative to the broader market or its sector coverage. Bearish coverage initiations from prominent Wall Street institutions often weigh on investor sentiment, signaling caution regarding a company's outlook. The negative rating prompted selling pressure as market participants reacted to the firm's cautious assessment.

By partnering with OpenAI, Getty is securing a new distribution channel and monetizing its vast archive in the AI era. Under the agreement, ChatGPT will pull from Getty's licensed catalog when users request visual responses, providing OpenAI with high-quality, legally cleared imagery. data.title: Strive reportedly targets 500 Bitcoin purchase this week funded by preferred stock sales
data.description:
Strive Inc., the Nasdaq-listed firm co-founded by Vivek Ramaswamy, is planning to acquire 500 Bitcoin this week, funded through sales of its Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Preferred Stock, known by its ticker SATA. The purchase would add to what has already become one of the most aggressive corporate Bitcoin accumulation campaigns on public markets.

The company has built its Bitcoin war chest almost entirely through a financial instrument most retail investors have never heard of: a preferred stock that trades near its $100 par value and pays a 13% annual dividend, distributed daily on business days.

As of September 8, 2026, Strive's total Bitcoin holdings stood at 24,531 BTC. The company's most recent disclosed purchase added 1,375 BTC for approximately $109 million, working out to an average price of roughly $79,281 per coin.

Strive managed to amass over 24,000 BTC in roughly one year. A significant chunk of that total, around 5,000 BTC, came through Strive's merger with Semler Scientific, but the rest has been ground out through a disciplined weekly buying program.

Roughly 70% of the capital deployed for Bitcoin purchases has come from SATA preferred stock sales. The SATA notional outstanding reached approximately $999 million as of early September 2026, meaning the company has nearly hit the billion-dollar mark in preferred stock issuance alone.

CEO Matt Cole has described the company's approach as buying Bitcoin "hand over fist."

Investors buy preferred shares at $100 a pop, collect a 13% annual yield paid out daily, and Strive takes the proceeds and converts them into Bitcoin. At a 13% annual payout on nearly $1B in outstanding preferred stock, the company is on the hook for roughly $130 million per year in dividends.

The structure also solves a problem that has plagued other corporate Bitcoin buyers. Companies like MicroStrategy pioneered the convertible debt approach to funding Bitcoin purchases, but convertible notes come with maturity dates and conversion mechanics that can create pressure at inopportune moments. Perpetual preferred stock, by contrast, has no maturity date. Strive never has to pay the principal back, it just has to keep meeting dividend payments.

The corporate Bitcoin treasury trend has evolved considerably since MicroStrategy first started buying in 2020. Strive's 24,531 BTC position places it firmly among the largest corporate holders.

Rather than making splashy one-time buys, Strive has settled into a pattern of consistent weekly accumulation. The key risk remains concentration. Strive has effectively become a leveraged Bitcoin vehicle wrapped in a corporate shell. If Bitcoin enters a prolonged downturn, the company would still owe 13% annual dividends on nearly $1B in preferred stock while sitting on a depreciating asset.

data.title: US yields rise after inflation data fuels rate hike bets
data.description:
Key points:
  • Traders lift odds of Fed hike next week to 86.8% from 67.5%
  • Benchmark 10-year yield at highest levels since October 2023
  • August CPI rises 0.4% month-on-month and 3.4% year-on-year

By Sinéad Carew and Karen Brettell

Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields approached 5% on Friday, trading at their highest levels since October 2023, after U.S. consumer price inflation accelerated, boosting expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.

Yields have jumped recently, as soaring oil prices renewed concerns about inflation, which is already running well above the U.S. central bank's target. A still-solid U.S. economy and heavy corporate and Treasury debt supply have added to the move, along with concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory.

Some analysts view 5% on the 10-year note as a critical line that could make bonds more competitive against stocks. Higher Treasury yields also flow through to the broader economy through costlier mortgages, auto and consumer loans, and more expensive corporate and municipal borrowing.

The benchmark 10-year yield briefly touched 4.9915% on Friday after data showed U.S. consumer prices sped up last month as the cost of gasoline rebounded after two straight monthly declines. The Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4% in August after rising 0.1% in July. In the 12 months through August, consumer prices rose 3.4%.

In response, traders ramped up bets that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points on September 16 at its two-day meeting, to an 86.8% probability from 67.5% before the release, according to LSEG data.

Friday's volatility coincided with a decline in oil prices. After an eight-session advance, U.S. crude futures (Clc1) settled down 2.4% at $100.05 per barrel.

Bank of America, Barclays, Wells Fargo and TD Securities were among the banks that said they now expect the Fed to hike rates next week.

"The first hike is just the beginning of the journey," said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. "There will be multiple hikes down the road to really rein in the inflation problem."

While yields pulled back from their session highs, Alvarado said that "until investors have confidence inflation will head back to the 2% goal, the path is wide open for the 10-year to reach 5%."

The yield on benchmark U.S. 10-year notes was last up 2.29 basis points at 4.967%, while the 30-year bond yield fell 1.1 basis points to 5.35%.

The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, rose 8.6 basis points to 4.636%.

A closely watched part of the U.S. Treasury yield curve measuring the gap between yields on two- and 10-year Treasury notes, seen as an indicator of economic expectations, was at a positive 32.9 basis points, after touching its flattest level since July 29.

"The constant upward pressure on bond yields also suggests that the bond market thinks the Fed is behind the curve," said Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management. "The Fed may still prefer to stay on hold and see whether inflation pressures eventually fade, but the bond market seems increasingly unconvinced."

While August CPI might not be enough to push the Fed to hike rates in September, Snyder said that "with oil prices hovering around $100 a barrel, it is hard to envision the inflation outlook getting much better in the near term."

data.title: Five Warning Signs the AI Stock Bubble Is in Its Final Stages — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Teresa Rivas

Stocks' rough patch doesn't mean the rally is at an end, but it could signal the finish line is closer than bulls hope.

The S&P 500 has had a difficult month: As of Thursday's close it had fallen 2.7% from its record close of 7798.99, reached on August 13. Part of that may be typical seasonal weakness, since August is historically a difficult month for the market, as is September. But with the index still up more than 10% so far in 2026, on track for its fourth year of double-digit gains, some investors are naturally questioning whether the recent declines indicate that the artificial intelligence-fueled run is finally starting to lose steam.

Capital Economics Senior Markets Economist James Reilly thinks that while that's unlikely to happen this year, the end may not be far off: "Looking across a range of equity market 'bubble' indicators supports our view that while the S&P 500's rally has further to run this year, its medium-term prospects are poor given how frothy the market looks," he writes in a note Thursday.

The range of factors his firm tracks shows that even if things are unlikely to come to a head now, the AI boom may be entering its final stretch. "They suggest the AI equity boom is in its final stages...the data look consistent with a late-stage bubble," Reilly writes.

Out of eight indicators, five are now at extremes that are consistent with equities nearing a peak.

Valuation is a red flag. Although the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio is now around 21 times, having pulled back from its late 2025 peak of 23 times, and U.S. valuations have fallen relative to those in markets elsewhere, there was a similar pattern of U.S. underperformance from 1999 to 2000. That means the recent pullback "is hardly a surefire sign the U.S. market is not in a bubble."

Likewise, that multiple still implies "very punchy earnings growth," as Reilly puts it.

Consensus earnings per share for the next 12 months are now at levels that correspond with the peak of the dot-com bubble, and unlike prior instances, the lofty forecasts can't be explained away by a rebound from prior weakness. The fact that so much of this expected earnings growth is projected over the long term and concentrated in the tech sector makes this doubly concerning, he writes.

Speaking of tech, the current S&P 500 "concentration is alarming," he notes, as the weights of the largest companies-all of which are tech-related-are at extreme levels. Both Nvidia and Apple recently accounted for more than 7% of the S&P 500, while Microsoft accounted for more than 5%.

Tech is also behind the next worry: Equity issuance is booming, another hallmark of a late-stage bubble. That metric could look even more extreme as AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic move toward highly anticipated initial public offerings.

And finally, foreign interest in U.S. equities has surged, much like it did before prior peaks.

The other three factors-corporate fundamentals, volatility and leverage-aren't at extremes that would signal trouble. However, with valuation, earnings, index concentration, equity issuance, and foreign ownership of U.S. stocks all flashing red, Reilly warns trouble could be creeping closer.

He predicts the S&P 500 will rally to 8250 by the end of the year, but fall back to 6500 by the end of 2027.

Investors should enjoy the party while it lasts.

Write to Teresa Rivas at teresa.rivas@barrons.com

data.title: Soybean Futures Fall After USDA Raises Outlook for 2026 Crop — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Kirk Maltais

  • Soybeans for November delivery fell 2.5% to $12.99 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade Friday, falling under the $13-a-bushel mark after the USDA's September WASDE showed higher production and yield forecasts for 2026.
  • Wheat for December delivery fell 2% to $7.26 1/4 a bushel.
  • Corn for December delivery fell 0.3% to $5.32 a bushel.

HIGHLIGHTS

Bigger Crop: Friday's WASDE report showed a larger U.S. soybean crop than forecast at this time last month. The USDA pegged 2026 soybean production at 4.54 billion bushels, with a yield of 52.8 bushels an acre. Last month, the USDA projected production at 4.52 billion bushels, with a yield of 52.7 bushels an acre. The report also showed higher export figures on strong demand from China, offsetting the higher production figures, AgResource said in a note.

Dour Start: CBOT grain futures pared early morning losses in trading just ahead of the WASDE, only to give way to a collapse in prices after the report came out. "I feel this is a function of yesterday's action being way over done to the upside as most of the strength yesterday was lead from crude oil," AgMarket.net's Cory Bratland said in a note.

Black Sea Blues: The USDA reduced its export projections for Russian and Ukrainian wheat crops for the 2026/27 marketing year in its WASDE report. The agency lowered its outlook for Russian exports by 3 million metric tons, to 43 million tons. It also cut its outlook for Ukrainian wheat exports by 1 million tons, to 12.5 million tons. The cuts to exports are seen as reflecting the additional supply chain strain coming from an escalated conflict between the two countries, Mike Castle of StoneX said in a note.

INSIGHT

Shifting Gears: The lasting impact of the WASDE isn't expected to linger long in the minds of grain traders, the Hightower Report said in a note. "Without a surprise in this report, the market will quickly return to trading other fundamentals such as South American weather and China demand, which has been very strong this week," the firm said in a note, in reference to soybean market conditions. Corn futures are also not expected to rally much on the report's data.

Beating the Spread: Export sales of U.S. corn beat analyst forecasts for the week ended Sept. 3, according to USDA data. Corn export sales for the 2026/27 marketing year totaled 1.93 million metric tons, topping the high end of forecasts from analysts surveyed by The Wall Street Journal, who placed sales at 700,000 tons to 1.7 million tons. Soybean sales landed on the high side of analyst forecasts for the week, at 2.64 million tons for 2026/27. Wheat sales for were 194,200 tons, which was below the range of forecasts from analysts surveyed.

AHEAD

  • The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
  • The USDA will release its weekly Crop Progress report at 4 p.m. ET Monday.
  • The EIA will release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update report at 10:30 a.m. ET Wednesday.

Write to Kirk Maltais at kirk.maltais@wsj.com

data.title: Jimmy Kimmel, Disney in talks to renew late-night show for another year
data.description:
Jimmy Kimmel and his employer, Disney-owned ABC, are reportedly in negotiations to extend “Jimmy Kimmel Live” for another year, according to Variety, just days after Page Six said the late-night host was making the current TV season his last.

Kimmel’s current one-year contract is a sharp cut from his previous three-year deal, as late-night audiences decline, advertising dollars dry up, and production costs rise.

Earlier this week, reports circulated that Kimmel’s show would not be renewed after a 24-year run following a tumultuous 12 months that saw the host suspended for comments surrounding Charlie Kirk’s assassination, increased regulatory pressure from the Federal Communications Commission, and his ongoing public feud with President Trump.

A source familiar with the situation told Page Six, “His contract is not getting extended,” a claim an ABC spokesperson swiftly denied.

“This information is inaccurate—any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative.”

Jimmy Kimmel’s current contract ends in May 2027.
